title: Lesson 70: Reliability Engineering: SLIs, SLOs, Error Budgets, and Runbooks for Agent Operations
description: The reliability-engineering toolkit: SLIs that measure user experience, SLOs that contract it, error budgets that decide when a bad week stops releases, and runbooks that tell a calm stranger what to do.

questions.question: A team sets its solution SLO equal to the platform SLA. What goes wrong with that choice?
options: A solution SLO should always exceed the platform SLA by a wide margin to be meaningful to users, to demonstrate engineering rigor, and to satisfy auditors.
Platform downtime then consumes the entire error budget, leaving nothing for the application-layer, integration, and maintenance failures the team owns.
The platform SLA is a hard ceiling that a solution SLO can never legally match or exceed in any measurement window.
Equal targets are correct, because the two numbers measure the same thing over the same period and window.
questions.explanation: When the solution SLO equals the platform SLA, any platform outage eats the whole error budget and the team's own failure classes have nothing left to spend, so the solution target is set deliberately below the platform number.

questions.question: What does a well chosen service level indicator measure?
options: The user's actual experience, such as the share of requests that succeed within an acceptable time.
Whether the servers hosting the service are powered on and reachable from the network at any point during the measurement window.
The count of every error a user could cause, including invalid input they typed into a form.
The internal CPU and memory counters of each component in the deployed architecture.
questions.explanation: An SLI measures how well the service is doing from the user's point of view, such as a success rate or a latency threshold, not an internal counter or raw uptime that a person would never feel.

questions.question: When a service has blown its error budget over the trailing window, what does the policy require?
options: Nothing changes at all, because reliability work and feature work are funded from separate and unrelated allowances.
The team permanently freezes all changes, including critical fixes, until the start of the next quarter.
The team halts non-critical changes and focuses on restoring the service until it is back inside its SLO.
The service is retired and rebuilt on a new architecture before any further release is permitted.
questions.explanation: The error budget governs release decisions: while a service is inside its SLO releases proceed, and once it has blown the budget the team halts non-critical changes until reliability work brings it back inside the target.
